analysis.one_liner: Makes granted patents much harder to invalidate and easier to enforce, while letting the FTC punish bad-faith patent demand letters.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat with cosponsors from both parties, got a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in April 2018 but never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how patents are reviewed and enforced. Once a patent is issued, it would be much harder to take away: challengers would face a higher burden of proof, fewer ways to start a review, and only companies actually accused of infringement could even ask for one. Courts would automatically presume that a winning patent owner deserves an injunction to shut down an infringer. It also creates fee breaks for universities and small inventors, gives small businesses faster court procedures, and makes it a federal offense for scammers to send bad-faith letters demanding payment over patents they don't honestly hold.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of already-issued patents — especially pharmaceutical, biotech, and patent-licensing companies — would keep their patents through fewer and harder-to-win challenges, and could more easily get court orders shutting down competitors. Universities and small inventors would pay lower fees and get help navigating patent lawsuits. Small businesses targeted by fraudulent demand letters would get an FTC enforcement tool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent owners, especially drug and licensing companies

how_it_helps.text: It requires patent-office review panels to apply the same presumption of validity used in court and forces challengers to prove a patent is invalid with 'clear and convincing' evidence, a much higher bar than the current standard, making reviews far harder to win.
It bars reviews unless the petitioner has actually been sued or charged with infringement, and generally allows only one review per claim, sharply limiting how many challenges can be brought.
It requires courts to presume that a patent owner who wins an infringement case suffers irreparable harm and deserves an injunction, making shutdown orders nearly automatic.
It expands liability for 'actively inducing' infringement and for supplying designs or instructions used to infringe overseas, even when the accused party didn't know the patent existed.

It lets the FTC treat bad-faith patent demand letters as deceptive practices, lets state attorneys general sue violators for up to $5 million, and bans demanding payment on patents already held invalid or expired.

It extends reduced 'micro entity' fees to university-affiliated inventors, expands a pilot program of patent-specialist courts with expedited procedures for small businesses accused of infringement, and requires the Patent Office to post its search tools and databases online for free.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that make, sell, or import products covered by someone else's patent — tech manufacturers, retailers, and generic drug makers — would face costlier litigation, a greater risk of injunctions halting their products, and broader liability even without knowledge of the patent. Consumers ultimately pay through higher prices built on patents that can no longer be cheaply reviewed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Accused companies and consumers paying patent-protected prices

drawbacks.text: Raising the invalidation standard in patent reviews to 'clear and convincing' evidence with a presumption of validity would protect weak patents that should not have issued, and the industries that must license around them — including generic drug makers — would pass those costs to consumers in the form of higher prices.

Presuming irreparable injury in every infringement case would replace judges' case-by-case judgment about whether shutting down a product serves the public, making product-blocking injunctions far more common.

The demand-letter title preempts existing state laws on patent demand letters and caps state attorney general penalties at $5 million per series of violations, which could displace tougher consumer-protection rules some states already enforce.
Holding someone liable for inducing infringement without requiring knowledge of the patent, and for products made abroad, would widen legal exposure for businesses that did nothing knowingly wrong.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: the bill addresses real abuses like repetitive petitions filed to harass patent owners and demand-letter scams, but the same changes also shield genuinely weak patents from scrutiny, and the bill's own findings concede that Congress is legislating on 'unintended consequences' of reforms it passed only in 2011.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The demand-letter crackdown and the small-business and university provisions are genuine, narrowly targeted benefits. But they are the smaller part of the bill. Its core effect is to make issued patents substantially harder to challenge and easier to enforce — a large and lasting transfer of market power to patent-holding industries, paid for by the companies that compete with them and by consumers who face higher prices, particularly for drugs. On balance, the costs outweigh the narrow benefits for the general public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee, got one hearing in April 2018, and was never voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Coons introduced the STRONGER Patents Act on June 21, 2017, joined by Senators Tom Cotton, Dick Durbin, and Mazie Hirono.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which held a hearing on April 18, 2018.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that build on, sell, or compete with patented products — including generic drug makers, tech manufacturers, and retailers — kept the current, cheaper system for challenging weak patents, and consumers avoided the higher prices that stronger, unchallengeable patents tend to produce. Patent owners gained nothing beyond the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that challenge patents, and consumers

for.name: Sen. Chris Coons
for.role: U.S. Senator from Delaware, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred (Chair: Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Held an April 2018 hearing but never reported the bill to the full Senate, so it never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but thin — one Democrat sponsor joined by two Democrats and one Republican — and the bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown of support or opposition exists in the record.

industries.note: Generic and biosimilar makers rely on the patent-office review process to knock out weak drug patents; the bill raises the evidence bar to 'clear and convincing', adds a presumption of validity, and bars reviews after a court ruling, making drug patents far harder to clear away. Consumers pay the difference in drug prices. (Source: bill text, S3)

industries.industry: Patent assertion companies and patent-licensing businesses
industries.note: Stronger infringement remedies, near-automatic injunctions, and a one-challenge limit make patents more valuable to assert against operating companies. The bill's demand-letter title, however, would curb the bad-faith letters some of these firms send. (Source: bill text, S3)

industries.industry: Product makers and retailers who implement others' patents (tech manufacturers, retailers, generic drug makers)
industries.note: These companies would face a harder path to invalidating patents used against them, near-automatic injunctions, and broader liability for induced infringement even without knowledge of the patent — costs ultimately passed to consumers. (Source: bill text, S3)

The bill extends reduced fees to university-affiliated inventors, gives small businesses expedited procedures in specialist courts, and makes Patent Office search tools free online. (Source: bill text, S3)
